impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis does not govern prior art determinations under AIA § 102(d)(2)—correctly determines when a reference patent is entitled to the filing date of its provisional application for prior art purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's finding that claims of the '409 patent were unpatentable as obvious and remanded for further consideration. The court addressed the critical question of whether, under AIA § 102(d)(2), a reference patent automatically receives the benefit of its provisional application's filing date or whether a written description analysis (as in Dynamic Drinkware) is required. This decision has significant implications for how prior art dates are established in inter partes reviews under the AIA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from potentially stricter standards for establishing prior art dates under AIA § 102(d)(2), making it harder for IPR petitioners to rely on provisional filing dates of reference patents without demonstrating adequate written description support.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies challenging patents in IPR proceedings may face increased difficulty in establishing early prior art dates for reference patents, potentially reducing the effectiveness of IPR as a tool for invalidating competitor patents.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement for broad method claims (here, a method of treating headache using any humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibody) requires disclosure enabling the full scope of the claimed genus, particularly where functional limitations define the claim breadth.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision addressing enablement standards for method claims covering a genus of antibodies for treating headache. Judge Dyk's dissent argued the panel's holding creates confusion about enablement for method claims, will undermine medical innovation by sustaining overly broad claims, and conflicts with Supreme Court precedent. The denial leaves intact a potentially permissive enablement standard for functionally-defined method claims in the biologics space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from a potentially broader scope of enforceable method claims, particularly for biologic therapies defined by functional limitations, allowing stronger exclusionary positions against competitors.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic and biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents on biologic therapies. The decision may sustain overly broad claims that impede follow-on innovation and market entry, increasing costs for companies developing competing biologics.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in asserted patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether the agreement terminated when the licensee shifted its business operations to patent enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that the licensee had not ceased business operations by shifting to enforcement activities, so the agreement had not automatically terminated. This decision clarifies the standing requirements for exclusive licensees in patent infringement suits.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees, including patent assertion entities and university spin-offs, benefit from confirmation that they can maintain patent infringement suits independently when their license agreements convey all substantial rights, even if their primary business shifts to enforcement.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potentially powerful defense—challenging standing of exclusive licensees—making it harder to dismiss suits brought by non-practicing entities operating under exclusive licenses from universities or other patent owners.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL of non-infringement and no damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement, and affirmed the damages award in a case involving communication systems using non-uniform constellations. The split treatment of eligibility across related patents provides important guidance on how § 101 applies to digital communication technology claims. The case was remanded for further proceedings on the vacated claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain implementation-focused claims and confirmation that damages awards based on properly qualified expert testimony will be upheld.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued uncertainty about § 101 eligibility for claims related to mathematical optimization techniques applied to communication standards, as the court vacated eligibility findings for some claims while upholding others from the same patent family.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses courts on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether claim construction of functionality in design patents involves factual questions that should be decided by a jury.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing on a design patent infringement case, with a notable concurrence defending the Egyptian Goddess framework and a dissent by Chief Judge Moore arguing the framework has been misapplied to improperly resolve infringement at summary judgment. The denial preserves the current design patent infringement analysis, including courts' ability to resolve infringement on summary judgment when the claimed and accused designs are sufficiently distinct.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the preservation of a framework that allows district courts to resolve design patent infringement at summary judgment when designs are sufficiently different, reducing litigation costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that courts will focus on differences between claimed and accused designs at summary judgment, potentially denying jury trials on infringement in cases where overall similarity arguments could be persuasive.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly excluded plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and whether a jury's breach of contract damages award should be reinstated after the district court set it aside.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment on trade secret damages and remanded for a new trial, instructing the court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury's award. The court affirmed the finding of trade secret misappropriation liability against Ford for developing competing software using Versata's proprietary technology. This case provides important guidance on trade secret damages methodology and the interplay between trade secret and contract claims in software licensing disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and trade secret owners benefit from the affirmance of misappropriation liability and the instruction to consider broader damages models, potentially increasing recoverable damages in trade secret cases involving licensed software.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop in-house alternatives to licensed software face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk, and the reinstated breach of contract jury award signals courts will defer to jury findings on contract damages.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's provision requiring payment 'if any Asserted Claim survives the EPR,' or whether it is purely a state-law contract dispute.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a dispute about whether T-Mobile owed a contingent payment under a patent litigation settlement agreement, because the contract interpretation question did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies the limits of Federal Circuit jurisdiction over post-settlement patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements may benefit from having contract interpretation disputes heard in regional circuits more experienced with general contract law rather than in the Federal Circuit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies drafting patent settlement agreements face uncertainty about which appellate court will hear disputes, potentially complicating forum selection strategies and increasing litigation costs when jurisdictional challenges arise.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a communications apparatus with a coupler for matching impedance to air are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), even if the claims are not indefinite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the final judgment of invalidity for the asserted patent claims, but on enablement grounds rather than indefiniteness. The court reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but agreed with Samsung that the claims failed the enablement requirement. This decision demonstrates that the Federal Circuit will independently evaluate alternative invalidity theories raised by defendants to affirm judgments of invalidity.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not relied upon by the district court, providing additional opportunities to defeat patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that even if they successfully defend against one invalidity theory on appeal, the Federal Circuit may invalidate their patents on alternative grounds raised by defendants.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court properly awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and sanctioned plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 for bringing a patent infringement suit where the patent's related applications had been rejected under § 101 following Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal without leave to amend and addressed the district court's award of attorney fees to Volkswagen and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel for pursuing a patent infringement suit where related patent applications had been rejected on § 101 grounds. The case highlights the risks of asserting patents whose family members have been rejected under Alice, and reinforces that courts may impose fees and sanctions when patentees pursue litigation despite clear eligibility problems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from strengthened fee-shifting and sanctions precedent that deters assertion of patents with known eligibility vulnerabilities, reducing the burden of defending against weak patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and their counsel face heightened risk of fee awards and sanctions when asserting patents whose related applications faced § 101 rejections, potentially chilling enforcement of patents in areas affected by Alice.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a defendant's motion for Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the patentee filed suit after related patent applications were rejected under § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and fees because the order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent infringement suit brought after the PTO had rejected claims in related applications on § 101 grounds following Alice. The court's decision requires district courts to adequately explain their reasoning when denying fee and sanctions motions in exceptional cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the requirement that district courts provide detailed explanations for denying fee motions, ensuring meaningful appellate review and potentially increasing the deterrent effect against frivolous patent suits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased scrutiny when asserting patents with related applications that failed § 101 review, as district courts must now more thoroughly address fee and sanctions requests.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulation imposing a 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping duty sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute and exceeds the agency's delegated authority.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's 15-day filing deadline for domestic interested parties in antidumping sunset reviews is a permissible exercise of agency authority. The court found the statute is silent on timing and that Commerce's regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking. This decision preserves an important procedural mechanism in trade enforcement that directly affects industries seeking to maintain antidumping duty orders.
impacts.positiveImplications: Foreign manufacturers and importers benefit from the preservation of a regulatory deadline that, if missed by domestic parties, can lead to automatic revocation of antidumping duty orders, potentially reducing tariff burdens.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic manufacturers face the continued risk of losing antidumping protection if they fail to meet the 15-day regulatory deadline, even though the statute itself does not impose such a deadline.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in patent claims directed to a float tool used in oil and gas wellbore operations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded a patent infringement judgment in a dispute between oilfield services competitors over a casing flotation device patent. The case turned on claim construction of 'internal diameter,' with the parties disputing whether the term could refer to both a measured diameter across the width and along the length of a pipe. The vacatur and remand will require the district court to reconsider infringement and validity determinations based on corrected claim construction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas technology space benefit from closer appellate scrutiny of claim construction, which may narrow the scope of asserted patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face the prospect of having favorable infringement judgments vacated when claim construction errors are identified on appeal, requiring costly retrials.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement action on both improper venue and failure to state a claim (§ 101 patent eligibility) grounds, or must transfer/dismiss for venue first without reaching the merits.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds under § 101. The patent related to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer.' AML argued that after finding venue improper, the court should not have also ruled on eligibility. The Federal Circuit's affirmance allows district courts to address multiple dispositive motions simultaneously, including merits-based eligibility determinations alongside venue challenges.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based invalidity rulings (such as § 101 ineligibility) even when venue is also improper, providing preclusive effect that prevents refiling in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders, particularly those asserting e-commerce patents, face the risk of receiving adverse eligibility rulings from courts that also lack proper venue, potentially foreclosing their ability to refile elsewhere.
